body_markdown:
McLaren has a lot of history to brag about, having won the motorsports trifecta of the Indy 500 (1972), the 24 Hours of Le Mans (1995), and the Formula 1 world driver and constructor championships (repeatedly). It is the Le Mans achievement, won with a Gordon Murray-designed F1 GTR sponsored by Ueno Clinic (a Japanese medical clinic specializing in penile cosmetic procedures) that its latest special edition—the 750S LM—commemorates.


In terms of modern roadgoing McLarens, this is the third LM special edition, the first being the 2015 650S LM and the second the 2020 720S LM. This new car is based on[the 750S, which came out for the 2024 model year](https://www.hagerty.com/media/new-car-reviews/2024-mclaren-750s-first-drive-supercar-state-of-the-art/) . As with those prior special editions, the new 750S LM’s upgrades are aerodynamic and cosmetic, but the headlining tweak is the flat-faced five-spoke wheel design that instantly recalls the seven[McLaren F1 GTR](http://facebook.com/reel/984819440161651) chassis that entered into the 1995 24 Hours of Le Mans. We’re told that McLaren owners have begged the company to make those wheels available as retrofits to other models, but thus far they remain exclusive to the LM series.


JAMES LIPMAN


JAMES LIPMAN


JAMES LIPMAN


Besides the wheels, the 750S LM receives a roof scoop reminiscent of the F1’s, though it just provides ambient cooling air to the engine compartment rather than induction air. Also, an MSO (McLaren Special Operations) high-downforce kit that includes a dual-airfoil front bumper, a revised active rear spoiler, and a louvered front fender panel. All told, it’s said to be good for a 10 percent increase in downforce. Gold brake calipers and center-lock nuts that are red for the left side and blue for the right side, just as on the ’95 Le Mans cars, complete the appearance package.


JAMES LIPMAN


Just two colors: Le Mans Grey which recalls the ’95 Ueno Clinic winner, and McLaren Orange, a vintage hue that is a bit quieter and flatter than the sparkly Papaya that is the brand’s signature color. Buyers could also spec between grey or orange Alcantara seat upholstery, optional unpainted carbon-fiber aero trim, and MSO billet pedals that, again, recall the race car.


JAMES LIPMAN


JAMES LIPMAN


Fifty of the model-year 2026 750S LMs have been built. If one isn’t currently headed to your driveway, keep an eye on the various auction sites for a used one because they are all sold out, we’re told. McLaren wouldn’t reveal the price, but it started at “just under $600,000.” Meaning that it was a substantial jump from the regular 750S’s $375,000 base price. And, as mentioned, the car does still offer extra-cost options, as all McLarens do.


## **Specs: 2025 McLaren 750S LM**


**Price:** $600,000 (est)
**Powertrain:** 4.0-liter twin-turbo V-8; seven-speed dual-clutch automatic transmission
**Output:** 740 horsepower; 590 pound-feet of torque
**Layout:** Mid-engine, two-door, two-passenger, rear-drive coupe
**Weight:** 3062 pounds
**0–60 mph:** 2.7 seconds
**EPA-rated Fuel Economy:** 17 mpg combined city/highway
**Competitors:** Ferrari 849 Testarossa;[Lamborghini Reveulto](https://www.hagerty.com/media/video/the-drivers-seat-henry-catchpole-on-the-lamborghini-revuelto/)


JAMES LIPMAN


McLaren invited a few journalists to sample an already sold 750S LM at the Thermal Club, a private motorsports complex east of Los Angeles. Except for some of the aforementioned detailing, the cockpit is straight 750. Meaning it works hard to evoke modern race tech with screens, knobs, and paddles. McLaren doesn’t busy up the steering wheel with controls like Ferrari, and the mode selectors for the transmission and stability control are mounted high on the instrument binnacle where they can easily be toggled by a finger.


JAMES LIPMAN


The “ordinary” 750S is already a state-of-the-art supercar. Its twin-turbo 4.0-liter V-8 flows the 740-horses worth of juice in a bawling and beautifully linear rush to the 8500-rpm rev cutoff. So quick and smooth do the revs spool that it’s easy to stray into the limiter in manual mode because you never feel the engine fall off as it rockets past its 590-pound-foot torque peak at 5500 rpm. In turbo engines, the amount of fun is directly linked to the amount of boost, and that can be a lumpy bed to lie in. Not so in the Mclaren 750S LM.


JAMES LIPMAN


JAMES LIPMAN


JAMES LIPMAN


Thermal’s north circuit is a technical and challenging playground, with fast esses, far-away apexes, knotty chicanes, some gently off-camber stuff, and one very long carousel that tested our patience as much as the front-end grip from the Pirelli Trofeo Rs. The 750S LM shines, especially in the brake department which hauls the circa-3100-pound car down from three digits with an unflappable repeatability.


Road-going McLarens once had hyper-kinetic steering—so-called “go-kart steering”—which was just how the Brits tend to like it. See: the[Lotus Elise](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ny47kkZkn_A) . The 750, like the 720, feels as if it’s gone to school a bit on Ferraris and Porsches and been calmed down to a more organic and natural heft and quickness. It delivers exactly the vectors you want and at efforts precisely calibrated to supply the requisite feedback you need.


JAMES LIPMAN


GIven that our test car was already sold and owned by a local, we were always accompanied by an instructor and not allowed to turn off the stability control from its top Track setting. In most cars that’s not a problem, as many of today’s track-mode systems lurk quietly in the shadows, allowing at least some sideways thrills before they intervene. Which makes them good teaching tools; you can’t learn if you can’t make any mistakes before the computer steps in to save you. And fast cars should be good teaching tools.


This is not McLaren’s philosophy. Its system is all about results. It begins massaging the car’s line almost from the moment it detects slip. In the long carousel, if you bomb in with just a hair too much throttle, the inside front brake starts cycling to squelch the understeer and pull you toward the apex. On a corner exit, it does the same in the back to keep the rear firmly planted behind the front. It’s like a football coach who goes to the line with the team and constantly barks instructions as the ball snaps. You might score more points that way, but your players won’t be happy. If the driver puts it in “Track,” it should mean Track and that the computer doesn’t grab the wheel unless it’s strictly necessary to keep you off the guardrails.


JAMES LIPMAN


The problem may be one of semantics; what McLaren calls Track would in some other cars be just an enhanced Sport mode. To get the 750S LM’s computer to back off, you must engage the multi-setting Drift Mode, which we weren’t allowed to do, either.


Nitpicks aside, the 750S LM is a thrilling and nostalgic plaything for hard-core McLaren fans and proof that the Woking works is in no danger of forgetting its illustrious history.


## **2025 McLaren 750S LM**


**Highs:** An animal on the track and a house cat on the street. Really does evoke the look of the F1 racers. Likely will always be collectible.


**Lows:** Interfering nannies in Track mode. A lot of extra money for what is largely an appearance package.


**Takeaway:** The 750S is a special car, and the LM version even more so. McLaren’s rich history still makes for a productive mine.


Eddy Eckart
